'''Lee Rupp''' (March 3, 1938{{spaced ndash}}September 20, 2025) was a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] politician from [[Nebraska]] who served as a member of the [[Nebraska Legislature]] from the 22nd district from 1983 to 1987.

==Early life==
Rupp was born in [[Monroe, Nebraska]], in 1938, and graduated from Monroe High School. He attended [[Northeast Community College|Norfolk Junior College]], and ultimately graduated from the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] with his bachelor's degree in agriculture. Rupp later received his master's degree in biology, and worked as a fisheries biologist for the [[Nebraska Game and Parks Commission]].<ref name="blue book">{{cite book|title=Nebraska Blue Book 1986-87|editor-last1=Smith|editor-first1=Gail Lynn|publisher=Clerk of the Nebraska Legislature|date=1987|url=https://govdocs.nebraska.gov/epubs/l3000/D001-198687.pdf|access-date=August 30, 2026}}</ref><ref name="remembered">{{cite news|last=Hammel|first=Paul|title=Former State Sen. Lee Rupp remembered for service to others, dedication to conservation|newspaper=Nebraska Examiner|date=September 24, 2025|location=|url=https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2025/09/24/former-state-sen-lee-rupp-remembered-for-service-to-others-dedication-to-conservation/|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref>

==Nebraska Legislature==
In 1982, when State Senator [[Donald Dworak]] declined to seek re-election, Rupp ran to succeed him in the 22nd district.<ref>{{cite news|title=Lee Rupp Opens 22nd Dist. Campaign|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=March 13, 1982|location=|page=8|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/205063505/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref> In the nonpatisan primary, Rupp faced former [[Humphrey, Nebraska|Humphrey]] City Councilman Francis Sand and farmer Dick Ternes.<ref>{{cite news|title=Nebraska Legislature|newspaper=[[Lincoln Journal Star|Lincoln Sunday Journal and Star]]|date=May 9, 1982|location=|page=5C|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-lincoln-star/194411308/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref> Rupp placed second in the primary, winning 33 percent of the vote to Sand's 41 percent, and they advanced to the general election.<ref name="1982 results">{{cite book|title=Official Report of the Nebraska State Canvassing Board, Primary Election, May 11, 1982, General Election, November 2, 1982|last=Beermann|first=Allen J.|publisher=Nebraska Secretary of State|year=1982|url=https://govdocs.nebraska.gov/epubs/S1200/S001-1982prim_gen.pdf|access-date=August 30, 2026}}</ref> Rupp defeated Sand with 53 percent of the vote.<ref name="1982 results"/>

Rupp ran for re-election in 1986, and was challenged by Ternes. In the primary election, he received 58 percent of the vote to Ternes's 42 percent.<ref name="1986 results">{{cite book|title=Official Report of the Nebraska State Canvassing Board, Primary Election, May 13, 1986, General Election, November 4, 1986|last=Beermann|first=Allen J.|publisher=Nebraska Secretary of State|year=1986|url=https://govdocs.nebraska.gov/epubs/S1200/S001-1986prim_gen.pdf|access-date=August 30, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Eglseder|first=Joanne|title=Rupp 'gratified' by primary vote margin|newspaper=[[Columbus Telegram]]|date=May 14, 1986|location=|page=1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-columbus-telegram/205063646/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref> Rupp defeated Ternes in the general election with 58 percent of the vote.<ref name="1986 results"/> During his tenure in the legislature, Rupp advocated for wildlife protection and conservation bills.<ref name="true Nebraskan">{{cite news|last=Kiser|first=Andrew|title=A true Nebraskan'|newspaper=[[Columbus Telegram]]|date=September 25, 2021|location=|page=A1, A7|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-columbus-telegram/205063977/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref>

In 1987, Rupp applied to be the director of the Game and Parks Commission and the vice president for university relations at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]],<ref>{{cite news|last=Peterson|first=Hazel|title=Rupp seeks jobs as lobbyist, head of Game and Parks Commission|newspaper=[[Columbus Telegram]]|date=November 25, 1987|location=|page=1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-columbus-telegram/205063724/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref> and was ultimately selected for the position at the University of Nebraska. He resigned his seat in the legislature, effective December 31, 1987,<ref>{{cite news|title=Sen. Rupp to resign his legislative seat|newspaper=[[Lincoln Journal Star|Lincoln Star]]|date=December 8, 1987|location=|page=18C|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-lincoln-star/205063796/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref> and Governor [[Kay Orr]] appointed [[Helen Campbell]] as his successor.<ref>{{cite news|title=Helen Campbell to succeed Rupp|newspaper=[[Lincoln Journal Star|Lincoln Journal]]|date=December 30, 1987|location=|page=1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/lincoln-journal-star/205063895/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref>

==Post-legislative career==
Rupp served as the vice president for university relations at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] until 1997, when he retired. He was succeeded by State Senator [[Ron Withem]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Hord|first=Bill|title=Sen. Withem To Quit Post In Nebraska|newspaper=[[Omaha World-Herald]]|date=October 23, 1997|location=|page=16|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/omaha-world-herald/205064124/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=September 1, 2026}}</ref> In 2021, the Game and Parks Commission renamed the Looking Glass Wildlife Management Area, near his hometown of [[Monroe, Nebraska|Monroe]], the Lee Rupp Wildlife Management Area in his honor.<ref name="true Nebraskan"/>

==Death==
Rupp died on September 20, 2025, at the age of 87.<ref name="remembered"/>
